transcript:
Header: 2026-04-15 14:00 PT | Duration: 55 mins | Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Nora Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Gupta (Redwood Platform), Rachel Li (Sigma CTO), Ben Carter (ML Eng), Marta Ruiz (Infra)

Summary: quick overview, then deep technical Q&A and action items.

[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Rachel Li: Rachel here.
[00:07] Ben Carter: Ben.
[00:09] Marta Ruiz: Marta.
[00:12] Nora Patel: Nora from Redwood.
[00:15] Alex Kim: Cool, goal for today is to walk through throughput tuning for your production workload - continuous batching, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs, token limits, and KV cache tuning. We'll also touch on quantization tradeoffs for latency.
[02:03] Ben Carter: Quick context - current prod is hosted on our k8s cluster, model is a 13B open-arch variant, p99 latency target is 250ms for short responses (~50 tokens), we see tail spikes during bursts.
[03:10] Nora Patel: Got it. What does your current batching look like? Are you using a max_num_seqs cap or relying on dynamic batching?
[03:45] Ben Carter: We're using a naive batching approach in our proxy - basically 5s batching window, which hurts latency. We set max_batch_tokens to 4096 but it's not ideal.
[04:30] Samir Gupta: 5s window is pretty long, that explains spikes. With continuous batching you want tight latency SLOs and a scheduler that drains partial batches if latency budget is close.
[05:05] Rachel Li: Can Redwood's scheduler do that?
[05:12] Nora Patel: Yes - we have knobs: max_num_seqs (max sequences per batch), max_total_tokens_per_batch, and a latency_deadline_ms which will force dispatch of partial batches. Example defaults: max_num_seqs=64, max_total_tokens=16384, latency_deadline_ms=60.
[06:00] Ben Carter: That latency_deadline_ms sounds useful. How do we pick values?
[06:15] Nora Patel: Typically you profile seq length distribution. If most requests are 20-60 tokens, set max_num_seqs higher and keep max_total_tokens to avoid OOM. For shorter SLOs reduce latency_deadline to 30-40ms so batches don't wait.
[07:30] Alex Kim: Also continuous KV cache helps for streaming contexts with repeated prefixes - it can dramatically reduce compute for token continuation. But cache hits depend on request pattern and how you shard cache across workers.
[08:10] Marta Ruiz: We're worried about KV cache memory across nodes in VPC/on-prem. How is it managed?
[08:30] Nora Patel: KV cache is per-inference-worker, but you can enable shared remote cache (Redis-like) - tradeoff is network hop latency. For on-prem we suggest co-locating cache on same rack or using NVMe-backed local cache to reduce hop. You also can evict by LRU and set max_cache_entries per model.
[09:50] Ben Carter: For quantization - we saw 4-bit gives big perf wins but quality degraded. What's your recommendation?
[10:10] Samir Gupta: Right, quantization tradeoffs depend on model and eval prompts. We recommend progressive approach: FP16 -> int8 -> 4-bit, with eval harness run on your prompt set and comparing embeddings and logits. For throughput we usually see 1.8-2.5x token/s improvements from int8 on Ampere GPUs; 4-bit has more variability.
[11:45] Rachel Li: Any scheduler knobs specifically for stability under bursts?
[12:00] Nora Patel: Yes - burst_capacity tokens allows short-lived oversubscription, and worker_thread_affinity pins batches to fewer workers to improve KV cache locality. Also set per-worker_queue_limit to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[13:40] Ben Carter: Example concrete numbers would help.
[13:50] Nora Patel: For your profile (median 40 tokens, p95 120), we might start with: max_num_seqs=96, max_total_tokens=8192, latency_deadline_ms=40, burst_capacity=20% of worker capacity, per_worker_queue_limit=8. That tends to maximize throughput while keeping p99 under 300ms.
[15:30] Alex Kim: We'll share a tuning doc with examples and a scheduler knobs matrix.
[15:40] Rachel Li: Regarding VPC, we need to ensure KMS and audit logs stay inside our VPC - does Redwood Private support that?
[15:55] Nora Patel: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM; in on-prem you can run our control plane locally. We'll share our security pack.
[17:20] Marta Ruiz: In terms of multitenancy, if we run Dedicated pools, can we reserve GPUs for bursty endpoints?
[17:40] Samir Gupta: Yes - reserved capacity + autoscale policies let you carve baseline and allow burst to shared pools. Also can set routing policies to prefer cheaper variants if baseline is saturated.
[19:05] Ben Carter: If we limit max_num_seqs high, do we risk OOM in KV cache?
[19:20] Nora Patel: Higher batch sizes increase total KV memory needed per batch - you should cap max_total_tokens and enable kv_cache_eviction_strategy. Also monitor kv_cache_hit_rate metric in Console; we can set alerts if memory climbs.
[20:55] Alex Kim: Let's walk through a live example - Nora, can you sketch how we'd tune for their p95 token lengths?
[21:10] Nora Patel: Sure - with sample distribution you sent (median 38, p95 118, p99 420), we set max_num_seqs to cover typical concurrency per GPU. If you typically have 16 concurrent users per GPU, max_num_seqs 96 is fine. Keep max_total_tokens modest to 8192 so p99 long responses don't block. latency_deadline set to 40ms to avoid waiting.
[24:00] Ben Carter: About continuous batching - does Redwood merge streaming and non-streaming requests?
[24:18] Samir Gupta: We separate streaming vs non-streaming paths if strict latency for first token is required; otherwise they can join same pool but streaming may get priority scheduling.
[25:30] Rachel Li: We have some long-form generation jobs (2k tokens) and many short queries. How to avoid long jobs blocking?
[26:00] Nora Patel: Use token limits and routing: route long-form to a separate pool with higher batch_size and different latency_deadline, or enforce max_tokens_per_request and chunk long responses with async streams.
[27:50] Ben Carter: Any recommended observability metrics we should export?
[28:10] Nora Patel: p50/p95/p99 latency, batch_size distribution, kv_cache_hit_rate, per-worker_gpu_util, queue_time_ms, tokens_per_second, and eviction_count. We'll onboard these into your Grafana with our agent.
[30:05] Alex Kim: Let's cover a few failure scenarios - tail latency spikes when batch size grows unexpectedly.
[30:25] Samir Gupta: Often caused by skewed seq lengths. Solution: clamp max_total_tokens and enable latency_deadline. Also consider adaptive batching that decays batch wait time when queue_time_ms grows.
[31:40] Rachel Li: How about quantization compatibility with KV cache?
[31:58] Nora Patel: KV cache format changes slightly with quantized kernels; our runtime supports transparent cache format conversion at load time but you pay a small conversion cost. For high-throughput you want to pin model variant to avoid conversions.
[33:20] Ben Carter: Can we pilot on a dev cluster?
[33:30] Alex Kim: Yes - Nora will run a 1-week benchmark with your sample load. We'll also provide a fork of our benchmarking harness.
[33:55] Rachel Li: For the pilot, what's the expected data we need to share?
[34:05] Nora Patel: Sample request traces with timestamps, seq length distribution, desired SLOs, and a representative prompt set for quality evals. Anonymize PII.
[35:40] Ben Carter: Any gotchas for on-prem networking?
[35:55] Samir Gupta: Ensure MTU and RDMA config for GPUs if using NVLink across hosts; otherwise, prefer local NVMe cache and limit remote cache hops. Also open specific ports for our control-plane sync if running Private.
[37:12] Marta Ruiz: Do you have guidance on setting worker thread counts?
[37:25] Nora Patel: Yes - thread count depends on GPU type and model. For Ampere 80GB with 8 cores we recommend 2-3 inference threads plus one IO thread. We'll include tuned examples in the doc.
[38:55] Alex Kim: Let's talk pricing tradeoffs of higher batch sizes - is there a cost penalty?
[39:10] Samir Gupta: Batching improves throughput so reduces per-token cost, but higher memory might require more GPUs; the console shows token-level cost so you can experiment.
[40:30] Rachel Li: On evals, we worry about quality regressions with int8 - how to detect?
[40:45] Nora Patel: Run automated evals: token-level perplexity, top-k similarity, and a small human eval set. Redwood Optimize can flag regressions against baseline on your prompts.
[42:00] Ben Carter: Any recommended defaults for max_num_seqs for 13B models?
[42:10] Nora Patel: Start 64-128 depending on concurrency. For your median lengths 96 is a good starting point.
[43:30] Alex Kim: OK we'll send the tuning doc and an initial recommended config.
[43:45] Rachel Li: What about security compliance for pilot?
[44:00] Nora Patel: We'll share SOC2 docs and the Private deployment checklist. If you need an on-site audit we can coordinate.
[45:20] Ben Carter: One last question - does Redwood support dynamic quantization at runtime per-request?
[45:35] Samir Gupta: Not per-request; quantized variants are model-level artifacts. We support model variant routing so you can route certain traffic to quantized variant.
[46:50] Alex Kim: Great. Any other questions?
[47:00] Rachel Li: No, thanks.
[47:05] Marta Ruiz: None from infra.
[47:15] Ben Carter: Good.
[47:30] Alex Kim: Recap: we'll share tuning doc, knobs, runner harness, and run a dev benchmark. Nora to own bench, Alex to own pricing/pilot template. Customer to share traces and prompt set.
[48:20] Rachel Li: Timeline looks good.
[48:40] Alex Kim: We'll send notes and next steps in an email. Thanks all.
[55:00] End of call.
